How to Close Duplicate Tabs in Chrome, Firefox and Edge

Opening the same document, search or video again is easy. Removing repeated copies makes the tab bar easier to navigate without clearing every page from a website.

By Michael Wester, creator of TabTools · 5 min read · Updated October 9, 2026

On this page

  1. Choose a method for your browser
  2. What counts as a duplicate tab?
  3. Close duplicate tabs in Chrome or Edge
  4. Use Firefox’s built-in duplicate commands
  5. Which copy does TabTools keep?
  6. Undo a cleanup and organise what remains
All guides

Quick answer

Open TabTools and click Close duplicates to remove repeated copies of a page across your normal browser windows. A pinned copy, a copy playing sound and the copy you are looking at stay open. Firefox also has built-in commands for closing duplicates of one tab or cleaning up duplicate tabs from its tab overview menu.

Choose a method for your browser

BrowserMethod covered here
ChromeOpen TabTools and select Close duplicates.
FirefoxUse its built-in duplicate commands, or select Close duplicates in TabTools.
Microsoft EdgeOpen TabTools and select Close duplicates.

Before a bulk cleanup, finish any unsaved work in repeated pages. Two tabs can show the same URL while holding different text you have entered into a form.

What counts as a duplicate tab?

Duplicate tabs are repeated copies of a page. Three copies of the YouTube homepage are duplicates; the homepage and two different YouTube search results are different pages from the same website.

TabTools compares whole addresses. Two tabs are duplicates only when everything matches, including the part after #. Many web apps keep the page there, so two different conversations in a mail app are not treated as copies. Letter case in the scheme and hostname is ignored. Letter case in paths and query strings, and the order of query parameters, remain significant.

Example URLsTabTools treatment
example.com/guide opened twiceDuplicates
example.com/guide#intro and example.com/guide#stepsDifferent addresses; both stay
example.com/guide and example.com/contactDifferent pages
example.com/search?q=tabs and example.com/search?q=bookmarksDifferent query parameters; both stay

Tracking parameters can make otherwise similar pages count as different addresses. One exception: a link that only tells the browser which words to highlight, ending in #:~:text= and some text, counts as the page itself. The command compares addresses; it does not inspect page content to decide whether two pages mean the same thing.

Close duplicate tabs in Chrome or Edge

The TabTools popup uses the same command in both browsers. These screenshots show Chrome with eight tabs, including three copies of the YouTube homepage.

  1. Install TabTools for Chrome or Microsoft Edge.
  2. Open the extension from the toolbar or extensions menu.
  3. Find Close duplicates under Suggestions. The number beside it is how many copies it would close. Click it.
  4. Check the result at the bottom of the popup. It reports how many duplicates closed and offers Undo for a few seconds. With no duplicates open, Close duplicates shows 0 and cannot be clicked.

You do not need to select the repeated tabs first. The cleanup covers normal windows within that browser, so two copies of a page can be matched even when they are in different windows. Private or incognito tabs are excluded.

Running the command in Chrome does not change Edge tabs, or vice versa. Use it separately in each browser if you have duplicates in both.

Use Firefox’s built-in duplicate commands

Firefox provides native options if duplicate removal is all you need.

  • For copies of one page: right-click the tab you want to keep and choose Close Duplicate Tabs.
  • For a broader cleanup: open List all tabs, then choose its duplicate-closing command, shown as Close all duplicate tabs or Close Duplicate Tabs depending on the interface.

Mozilla’s tab context menu guide explains the first option. Its tab overview menu guide describes the broader cleanup and says it keeps the last active tab among duplicates.

If you already use TabTools for Firefox, open its popup and click Close duplicates. Its matching and retention rules are the TabTools rules below; do not assume they are identical to Firefox’s native command.

Which copy does TabTools keep?

TabTools never closes a pinned copy, a copy that is playing sound, or the copy in view in its window. When one of those exists, the other copies close. When none does, it keeps the first copy in the browser’s tab order and closes the later ones.

It does not choose the newest tab or the tab you used most recently. A retained copy may therefore be in another window. With one pinned tab and two unpinned copies of a page, only the pinned tab remains.

If a page has several protected copies, for example two pinned ones, they all remain, so the command does not guarantee exactly one tab for every address.

Undo a cleanup and organise what remains

After the cleanup the popup shows the result with an Undo button for a few seconds. Undo reopens the tabs from that cleanup. It reopens pages by URL; unsaved page content is not guaranteed to return. Once the result has gone, open Recently closed at the bottom of the popup and click a tab to reopen it. That list holds the last 25 tabs TabTools closed and is cleared when the browser closes.

For different pages you have finished with, see how to close all tabs from the same website. For pages you want to keep, sorting tabs by website brings related tabs together without closing them.
